title: The Salt in the Water
word: the three doshas as a way of noticing
hookLine: a father hides salt in water. his son can't find it anywhere, and can taste it everywhere
carry: tat tvam asi: you are more than your type
tomorrow: Arjuna says the mind is as hard to hold as wind. what does Krishna say?
last: THE MIND IS MADE OF FOOD.

cards: Shvetaketu is still learning from his father. One evening, in the Chandogya Upanishad, Uddalaka hands him a lump of salt. Put this in water, he says, and come to me in the morning.
Morning comes: bring me the salt. The boy looks, and can't find it. It's dissolved.
Then sip from this end, his father says. Salty. Sip from the middle.
Salty. Sip from the far end. Salty.

teach.h: TAT TVAM ASI: YOU ARE THAT.
teach.b: Then Uddalaka says it. You can't see Being here, my dear, but it's here, all through. That finest essence is the self of everything.
That's what's real. That is the self. And then the three words Hindus have carried ever since: tat tvam asi.

You are that. This is the teaching of atman: under your body, your moods, your habits, there is a self that isn't any of them, and the Upanishad ties it to the Being that runs through everything, like the salt.
Hindu schools read just how closely in different ways. Now Ayurveda. Its classical texts ask two questions about a person, and a physician examines both.
Prakriti: a person's nature, their constitution, the banks of the river. Vikriti: how things stand now, the water level after a storm.
And prakriti is the same word Hindu philosophy uses for nature itself, everything that changes, and the Gita sets it beside the self that knows it.
So even Ayurveda's deepest question about you, what's your nature, is a question about the river. Tat tvam asi points to whoever is watching the river. That matters the day someone hands you a label.
A quiz says you're pitta, so you're intense, end of story. Hindu teaching would say: you do have a nature, and it's real, and how you are today changes by the afternoon.
But you aren't your nature. You are that. On this path there's no type quiz and no diagnosis; that belongs to trained practitioners.
What anyone can do is hold the label lightly, and ask how today is.

how: Ayurvedic practitioners consider both a person's nature (prakriti) and present state (vikriti); in Hindu teaching, from the Chandogya's 'tat tvam asi' onward, the self (atman) is more than either, and students of Vedanta meditate on that line as one of the great sayings. On this path there is no type quiz.

games.q: what does “the three doshas as a way of noticing” mean?
o: three fixed types that decide who you'll always be
three forces that shape a nature, but not the self
three rules for eating well, one for each meal

games.q: the salt and the river — tap the pairs.
p: a person's nature, the river's banks
how things stand now, the water level

s: Uddalaka's salt can't be seen but can be tasted everywhere
you don't see Being here, he says, but it's here.
in Hindu teaching, your dosha type is your deepest self
prakriti describes a nature. tat tvam asi points to the self under it.
this path offers a quiz to find your dosha type
no quiz and no diagnosis: just the question, how am I today?

games.q: a friend says: i'm kapha, so i'm just lazy, it's my nature. by the salt lesson, what fits?
o: agree: your type is who you are.
you have a nature, but you're more than it: tat tvam asi.
types are fake, so nature means nothing.
games.why: Ayurveda takes prakriti seriously. the Upanishad says the self runs deeper than any nature: you are that.

practice: Sit, and let the body be as it is today: warm or cool, heavy or light, busy or still. Each time you notice something, say inwardly, I see this. Then rest as the one who sees, the way the salt is in every sip.
If you pray, rest in the presence you pray to. If you like, repeat tat tvam asi quietly, a line Vedanta students meditate on.

wordCard.voice: The three doshas, as a way of noticing. Today, two questions about a person, prakriti and vikriti, and the older answer under both: tat tvam asi, you are that.

orig.note: Sanskrit: you are that. Uddalaka's refrain to his son in the Chandogya Upanishad, one of Hinduism's great sayings.

carryVoice: Your line: tat tvam asi, you are more than your type. The salt is in every sip. Same time tomorrow.
